analysis.one_liner: Removes federal endangered-species protection from plants and animals found entirely within one state.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would strip Endangered Species Act protections from species that never cross state lines, never got a hearing or a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill declares that any plant, fish, or wildlife species found entirely within a single state's borders — and not sold as a commodity — is not part of interstate commerce and cannot be regulated under the Endangered Species Act or any other federal law based on the Commerce Clause. In practice, it would take the federal government out of protecting rare species that live in only one state, leaving protection entirely to state governments. It was introduced by Sen. Mike Lee with three Republican cosponsors and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where it died without action.
analysis.who_benefits: Landowners and companies that develop, mine, log, or drill on land where an intrastate endangered species lives would no longer face federal permitting requirements, habitat protections, or restrictions under the Endangered Species Act. Removing a species from federal protection can clear the way for construction, grazing, water diversions, or resource extraction that federal listing would otherwise delay, condition, or block. State governments would also gain sole authority over these species, free from federal oversight.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Developers, miners, loggers, and energy firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill exempts any species found entirely within one state and not part of a national commodity market from regulation under the Endangered Species Act of 1973 and from any other law whose authority rests on the Commerce Clause.

Exemption from the Endangered Species Act removes the federal requirements — such as prohibitions on harming listed species and on destroying their habitat — that otherwise apply to landowners and project developers in the species' range.

analysis.who_pays: Species that exist only in one state would lose their federal safety net. If a state chooses not to protect a species — or lacks the resources to — nothing would prevent its extinction, and the loss is permanent. People who value wildlife, healthy ecosystems, and the recreational and scientific benefits of biodiversity would bear that cost, and future generations would inherit whatever disappears.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes federal protection from species that live in only one state, which is precisely where federal protection matters most: many of the nation's rarest plants and animals have small ranges, and a state that declines to protect them would leave the species with no safeguard at all.

Because federal listing triggers habitat protections that restrict how land can be developed, logged, mined, or grazed, the bill would eliminate the main legal brake on projects that could push a one-state species to extinction.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: some landowners face genuine costs when a federally listed species with a tiny range restricts their property, and states are capable stewards of their own wildlife. But the cost runs the other way and is one-sided — federal protection is the strongest tool preventing extinctions, and a species that loses it in an unwilling state is gone for good. The bill is written broadly (any law resting on the Commerce Clause, not just the Endangered Species Act), so its protections-stripping effect could extend well beyond endangered species. Weighed honestly, the risk of permanent species loss far outweighs the regulatory relief.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the Native Species Protection Act on March 14, 2024, with Republican Sens. Ted Cruz and Dan Sullivan as cosponsors.

The bill would exempt any species found entirely within a single state and not part of a national commodity market from the Endangered Species Act and any other regulation grounded in Congress's power over interstate commerce.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day of introduction.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was ever taken on the bill, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Endangered species with one-state ranges kept their federal protection, and the landowners and extraction and development interests who stood to be released from Endangered Species Act obligations gained nothing. The public interest in functioning ecosystems was the winner of the inaction.

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.role: U.S. Senator from Utah; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip federal protection from species found entirely within one state.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All four supporters — the sponsor and three cosponsors — were Republicans, and no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill.

industries.industry: Real estate developers and landowners with listed species on their property
industries.note: The bill died in committee, so developers never got the Endangered Species Act exemption it would have created. Had it passed, they would have been freed from federal restrictions on developing land where a one-state endangered species lives, at the cost of the species' survival.

industries.industry: Mining, logging, and oil and gas companies
industries.note: Federal listing of an intrastate species can restrict extraction and timber operations in its habitat; the bill would have removed that obstacle. Its death leaves existing federal protections in place.

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation and wildlife tourism businesses
industries.note: These businesses depend on intact wildlife and ecosystems, and the bill's failure preserves the federal rules that keep one-state species from going extinct.
